messages.subject: occuFP and missing data
parts:
It appears that there is a problem with occuFP when there are missing observations.  For example, using the data provided in the example on the occuFP help page, if I change one value of the data to NA and then try to fit a model using occuFP I get an error:
> y[1,1] <- NA
> umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y,site,occ, type = type)
> m1 <- occuFP(detformula = ~ METH, FPformula = ~1, stateformula = ~ habitat, data = umf1)
Error in if (any(y[, 1:sum(type[1:2])] > 1)) stop("Values of y for type 1 and type 2 data must be 0 or 1.") :
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
 
Although the error message is logical, this seems unintended, since the unmarkedFrameOccuFP allows for missing observations.  Also, it seems to me that missing observations could be accommodated in the likelihood function by just excluding those cases in the calculation.
 
I am also wondering if the backTransform method for occuFP allows a type argument to specify the probability of detections being certain (Pcertain)?

parts:
Dave;
Thank you so much.  I do have one other question.  I'm trying to figure out how to compare your 2-category detection model with the Royle-Link (2006) and MacKenzie et al (2003) models using AIC.  However, it appears that the likelihoods are not comparable, partly due to the data structure for your model differing from the other 2, and/or the use of binomial versus multinomial probabilities in the likelihoods.  I'm trying to see how to constrain your model to get to the Royle-Link model, but I'm stuck.  If I set b=0, forcing all detections to be uncertain, then the P11*b term in the likelihood becomes zero and I lose the other 2 categories.  I'm thinking what is needed is a completely new formulation for the likelihood.  Have you by chance given this any thought? 
Eric

messages.author: e256ba06197c185a
messages.subject: Re: occuFP and missing data
parts:
Eric -
 
You are correct that the way to constrain the multi-detection-state likelihood to get the Royle-Link model is to set b to equal 0 and the way to get the original MacKenzie model from the likelihood is to set b to equal 1. When Jim Hines set up the false positive model in Presence he only included the multi-detection-state formulation and to get the Royle-Link model or the multi-detection-method model from my paper you need to fix parameters.
 
I am not sure there would be anyway to compare AIC values between the R-L and multi-detection-state model because the latter by default includes extra information in the likelihood (whether the detection was 'certain' or 'uncertain'). It is possible to compare AICs between the R-L and MacKenzie model because all you need to do is fix p_10 to 0 to go from one to the other. It is also possible to compare multi-detection-state model where false positives are included to one where they are assumed not to occur by again fixing p_10 to equal 0. In this case b is still estimated and kept in the likelihood. These are different questions than yours though, having to do with whether there is support for false positives occurring rather than which model works best to model that process.
 
The comparisons between the R-L and MDS models I have done have been based on simulation and it seems like if you have the added information to run the MDS and it is accurate there is a general benefit to using that information (lower MSE). This assumes you have a good measure to call a detection certain or uncertain and you can model that process well.
